access_patterns.description: Fetch one notification by its id.
Fetch the search data rows of a list of post ids (IN list) with one BatchGetItem of up to 100 keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=post_id (one key per id in the IN list)

access_patterns.description: Delete every upload reference of one target (type and id): a Query on the target key reads the item keys, then BatchWriteItem deletes them.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=target_key (Query to find the items, then DeleteRequest per item)

access_patterns.description: Delete all quotes made by one post: a Query on post_id reads the item keys, then BatchWriteItem deletes them.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=post_id (Query to find the items, then DeleteRequest per item)

access_patterns.description: Fetch the settings row of one category.
Check whether a user has a do-not-disturb window covering now: Query the user's items with the sort key at or below now, filter ends_at above now, limit 1.
Fetch a user's bookmark of one target (type and id).
Set last_used_at on an existing API key; the condition stops the update from creating a missing item.
Fetch one group by id.
Check whether a user belongs to a group by reading the membership item.
Check whether any score of one score type exists: Query the type index with limit 1.
Fetch one user avatar row by id.
List the names of the tag groups of one category from the category's item collection (the group name is copied onto the link item).
List id, name and slug of the tags of one category from the category's item collection.
Delete all daily like counters of one user: a Query on user_id reads the item keys, then BatchWriteItem deletes them.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (Query to find the items, then DeleteRequest per item)

access_patterns.description: Delete all poll votes of one user: a Query on user_id reads the item keys, then BatchWriteItem deletes them.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (Query to find the items, then DeleteRequest per item)

access_patterns.description: Delete all topic views of one user: a Query on the viewer key reads the item keys, then BatchWriteItem deletes them.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=viewer_key (Query to find the items, then DeleteRequest per item)

access_patterns.description: Check whether a badge was granted within a time range: Query the badge index on badge_id with granted_at BETWEEN, limit 1.
Read the primary email row of a user: Query the user's EMAIL# items and filter on primary = true (a user holds one or two emails).
Read a topic by id (GetItem on the topics placeholder; the owner group defines the full item).
Read a non-deleted topic by id: GetItem, and the application drops the item when deleted_at is present.
Existence check of a timing row by topic, post number and user: GetItem on the full key.
Read the email address of a user's primary email: Query EMAIL# items of the user, filter primary = true.
Read the non-deleted actions of one user on one post: Query the ActionsByUserPost index on user_id and post_id, with a filter on deleted_at absent.
Check whether the user has another primary email than a given id: Query EMAIL# items of the user, filter primary = true and email_id <> :id.
Insert a timing row, ignoring an existing one (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING): PutItem that fails its condition when the key exists; the application treats the failure as the no-op.
Add elapsed milliseconds to an existing timing row: UpdateItem with an atomic ADD on msecs, conditional on the row existing (the source UPDATE does nothing for a missing row).
Existence check for any non-deleted action of a type: Query ActionsByType with Limit 1 and a filter on deleted_at absent.
Insert an email: one TransactWriteItems with the email item and the unique sentinel for (user_id, primary), each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists. The application generates the email id.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=EMAIL#email_id; sentinel PK=user_id AND SK=UNIQ#PRIMARY#primary

access_patterns.description: Delete an email by its id: look the item up in UserEmailsById (returns user_id and primary), then one TransactWriteItems deletes the email item and its sentinel.
Read the post number of a timing row by full key: GetItem.
Read all emails of a user: Query EMAIL# items of the user.
First non-deleted actions of a user ordered by id: Query the base table on user_id (sort key is the action id, ascending) with a limit and a deleted_at filter.
Delete all actions of a user: Query the base table on user_id (its partition key), then BatchWriteItem deletes in batches of 25 (a key-scoped delete, not a Scan).
Delete all timings of a user: Query PostTimingsByUser on user_id (returns table keys), then BatchWriteItem deletes in batches of 25 (about 5 rows per user).
Read the icon of every badge (55 rows): Query the BadgesAll index, whose single partition key value 'all' holds every badge.
Read a badge by its unique name: Query BadgesByName.
Fetch the live post with a given post_number in each of up to five topics. One key per topic_id; deleted posts (deleted_at set) are dropped by the application after the fetch.

Fetch a live post by id within a topic, restricted to a set of post types and ordered by sort_order. The id leads the PostsById key, topic_id is the sort key, post_type and deleted_at are a FilterExpression; one id returns at most one item, so the order is trivial.
Fetch one live post by topic_id and post_number; the item is dropped by the application when deleted_at is set.
Fetch one live post by its id alone; deleted_at is a FilterExpression.
Read the outbound_message_id of a post by id, ordered by created_at (one id, so one item).
Fetch one live post by id within a topic; deleted_at is a FilterExpression.
Look up a user by username through the UsersByUsername index, which projects the whole item.
Find a user id by lower-cased username through the UsersByUsernameLower index; the id is a table key attribute, so a KEYS_ONLY projection covers it.

Consistency repair of users.title: reset the title of a user whose granted title badge is no longer enabled or title-allowed. Served at write time: the owner write that changes the badge, the user's badge grant or the profile's granted_title_badge_id runs a conditional UpdateItem on the user item (Streams consumer for the fan-out), not a sweep over all users.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=id (merged design: key attribute id is user_id)

access_patterns.description: Orphan clean-up of users.uploaded_avatar_id: when an upload is deleted, a Query on the UsersByUploadedAvatar index finds the users that reference it and a conditional UpdateItem per user replaces the reference. Runs from the upload delete path or its Streams REMOVE event, not as a scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=uploaded_avatar_id (GSI Query to find users), then PK=id (UpdateItem) (merged design: key attribute id is user_id)

access_patterns.description: List the linkable ids of one user's sidebar links of one linkable type
Read one user profile by user id
Fetch id, title and slug of a list of topics by id (IN list), skipping topics with deleted_at set
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id (one key per id in the IN list; items with deleted_at set are dropped by the application)

access_patterns.description: Existence check of a topic by id with a given archetype and no deleted_at
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id (archetype equality and deleted_at absence checked by the application on the returned item)

access_patterns.description: Read highest_post_number of one topic
Read one upload by id
Find the upload with a given url and id above a cursor, then keep it when retain_hours is unset or the retention has passed and created_at is before a cutoff
Update the cooked bio and its version on one profile
Insert up to three links for a user, skipping a link that already exists (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING): one conditional PutItem per link
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=link_key ('<linkable_type>#<linkable_id>') (merged design: key attribute linkable_type is link_key)

access_patterns.description: Insert a user profile
Delete a user profile
Read the optimized image of an upload for an exact width, height and extension
Read the optimized images of an upload for a width and height, any extension
List the links of one sidebar section and linkable type in position order
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=linkable_type,sidebar_section_id AND SK position ascending (merged design: key attribute linkable_type is link_key)

access_patterns.description: Read the upload with a given sha1
Insert an optimized image; the table key (upload_id, variant) enforces the source's unique (upload_id, width, height, extension)
Update the url and updated_at of an optimized image, addressed by the upload_id and variant of the loaded record

Consistency repair: clear granted_title_badge_id on a profile whose user has no title. Modeled at write time: when the title of a user changes to empty, a conditional UpdateItem on that user's profile removes the badge reference
Insert an upload and its sha1 sentinel in one TransactWriteItems; a taken sha1 cancels the insert
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=upload_id; sentinel Put on upload_sha1_sentinels with PK=sha1

access_patterns.description: Set dominant_color on one upload
Look up one user by lower-cased username through the UsersByUsernameLower index.
Fetch users by id for lists of ids (author, participant and mention lookups); the key lists vary in length, so the read is a BatchGetItem of up to 100 keys.
Fetch one user by id.
List the ids of the users a user has muted; a member that also returns the muted users' usernames follows with a BatchGetItem on the users table.
Read a theme's fields of one type_id; the Query on the theme's partition filters on type_id.
Read a theme's fields by name and type_id; the Query on the theme's partition filters on both.
Read a theme's fields whose name is in a short list; the Query on the theme's partition filters on name.
Update a user's updated_at and last_posted_at by id. The item must exist, so the update does not create one.
Update value_baked of a theme field. The caller holds the field's theme_id and field_key from the load; the ThemeFieldsById index resolves them when only the field id is known. The item must exist.
Read one theme field by theme_id, target_id, type_id and name, the full unique key.
Insert a theme field. The table key is the source's unique key (theme_id, target_id, type_id, name), so the condition rejects a duplicate.
Insert a user and its uniqueness sentinels (username_lower, and secure_identifier when present) in one transaction of at most 3 items.
Read a theme's fields for a few target_ids and names: one Query per target_id on SK begins_with, filtered on name.
Read a theme's fields by name for one of two target_ids: one Query per target_id on SK begins_with, filtered on name.
Delete a user and its uniqueness sentinels in one transaction; the application reads the user first to know the sentinel keys.
Read the fields of a theme and target_id with a given name: Query on SK begins_with, filtered on name.
Read all fields of a theme.
Existence check for a theme's fields of one type_id: Query on the theme's partition filtered on type_id, projecting keys only.
Read the fields of a theme and target_id with a given name: Query on SK begins_with, filtered on name; the sort over a constant theme column is a no-op.
Read name and value of a theme's fields for one target_id; the application sorts the roughly 12 returned items by name and id.
Delete every group request of one user: Query RequestsByUser on user_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by id (25 items per call).
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI PK=user_id; then delete by PK=id

access_patterns.description: Delete every topic claim of one user: Query ClaimsByUser on user_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by topic_id. Serves the redesign requirement on reviewable_claimed_topics.user_id.
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI PK=user_id; then delete by PK=topic_id

access_patterns.description: Retention delete of stubs with a given status created at or before a cutoff: Query StubsByStatusAge with status equality and created_at range, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by id. No Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI PK=status AND SK created_at <= :cutoff; then delete by PK=id

access_patterns.description: Read the review groups of a post type for 8 categories: one Query per category_id (8 Queries) with SK begins_with the post type.
Read the sprite of one theme by theme_id (unique in the source).
List every model as name and id for a dropdown: Query the LlmModelsAll index on its constant partition value. The table holds 10 rows. No Scan.
Check whether a user owns an upload: GetItem on the unique (user_id, upload_id) pair.
Delete all fragment embeddings of one model: Query PK=model_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by full key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=model_id; then delete by PK=model_id AND SK=strategy_fragment

access_patterns.description: Delete all topic embeddings of one model: Query PK=model_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by full key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=model_id; then delete by PK=model_id AND SK=strategy_topic

access_patterns.description: Delete all post embeddings of one model: Query PK=model_id, then BatchWriteItem DeleteRequest by full key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=model_id; then delete by PK=model_id AND SK=strategy_post

access_patterns.description: Insert one scheduler run record; the id is generated by the application.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=id (item being written, with expires_at TTL attribute)

access_patterns.description: Complete a scheduler run: set duration_ms, live_slots_finish and success on the item by id.
Read all custom fields of one category, in id order.
Read the trackers of one identifier whose target differs from a given target.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=identifier AND SK <> :target (applied as a key-condition-free filter on target)

access_patterns.description: Read the active timer of one timerable and type with a given public_type.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=timerable_key; filter deleted_at not present AND public_type = :public_type

access_patterns.description: Read the fields of one post whose name is in a list of up to 7 names, in id order.
Read the active timer of one timerable and type with a given status_type.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=timerable_key; filter deleted_at not present AND status_type = :status_type

access_patterns.description: Read one tracker by identifier and target.
Read active timers of a type that are due (execute_at <= now) from the sparse DueTimersByType index; the application orders the few results by id.
Read name and value of all fields of one post, in id order.
Update last_run_at, next_run_at and last_success_at of a tracker; the source addresses it by id, the application addresses it by identifier and target.
Read the fields of up to 7 categories whose name is in a list of up to 10 names: one Query per category id with a name filter.
Find the categories that have a field with a given name and value, through the CategoryFieldsByName index (the key the redesign requirement assumes).
Read every attribute of all fields of one post.
Insert a post custom field; ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING becomes a conditional put that is skipped when the item exists.
Read all active timers of a type from the sparse DueTimersByType index; the application orders them by id.
Insert a tracker keyed by identifier and target; the key doubles as the uniqueness guard.
Retention delete of runs older than a cut-off: served by DynamoDB Time to Live on the expires_at attribute (started_at plus the retention period), with no application call and no Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=id (removed by TTL when expires_at passes)

access_patterns.description: Read the custom fields with a given set of names for a handful of topics: one Query per topic and name prefix, issued together by the application.
Existence check: does any watched word exist for an action. Query with Limit 1 on the action partition, returning keys only.
Read all custom fields of one topic, in field id order within each name.
Read the vote count item of one topic.
Read the vote count items of a list of topics with one BatchGetItem.
Existence check for an override by locale and translation key.
Read the notification schedule of one user (Limit 1).
Read one badge type by id.
Read one plugin store row by plugin name and key (Limit 1).
Record an applied migration version; the write fails when the version is already recorded.
Read a color scheme by id; the application discards the item when remote_copy differs from the requested flag.
List the words of one action in id order (sort key), with a row limit.
Read one badge type by id (Limit 1).
List all overrides of one locale.
List all applied migration versions in version order: a Query on the ledger partition, sorted by the version sort key.
Read one plugin store row by plugin name and key.
Write a skipped-email log item with an application-generated id and an expires_at epoch attribute for TTL.
Read a color scheme by id.
Read all enabled notification schedules from the sparse EnabledSchedules index, which holds only items with enabled_marker.

Retention delete of old skipped-email logs, served by Time to Live on expires_at instead of a scan and batch delete: DynamoDB removes expired items in the background at no write cost. Reads that must not see expired items filter on expires_at.
access_patterns.key_condition: TTL on expires_at (DynamoDB-initiated delete, no request)

access_patterns.description: Fetch the shared draft of one topic by topic id.
Fetch the full stats item of one user.
Fetch first_unread_at of one user with a ProjectionExpression.
List the ids of all user fields. Replaces the full scan with a Query on the single item collection that holds the 14 field definitions.
List the usernames of the users one user allows to send private messages. The username is copied onto each allow-list item, so the join to users is a single Query.
List the tag ids a user watches at one notification level, on the TagUsersByLevel index keyed on user_id and notification_level.
Upsert the search text of one user. PutItem replaces the item for the user_id key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (item written: user_id, raw_data, locale, version)

access_patterns.description: Read the revisions of one draft by user and draft key; the caller compares the item's sequence with the sequence it holds.
List the polls of one post in id order with a limit; the sort key is the poll id.
List all polls of one post.
Fetch the shared drafts of a list of topic ids (the source IN lists run up to 36 ids) with BatchGetItem, at most 100 keys per call.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id (one key per listed topic id)

access_patterns.description: Upsert the search text of one topic. PutItem replaces the item for the topic_id key.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id (item written: topic_id, raw_data, locale, version)

access_patterns.description: Read the notification level of a user for the tags of one topic: the application takes the topic's tag ids from the topic_tags owner's by-topic read, then runs BatchGetItem on tag_users for (user_id, tag_id), keeps levels 3 and 4, sorts them descending and takes the limit.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=tag_id (one key per tag of the topic)

access_patterns.description: Insert one compiled JavaScript cache record with its unique-value sentinels (theme_id and theme_field_id plus name, each written only when present) in one TransactWriteItems of at most 3 items.

Orphan clean-up of search rows for deleted topics: a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the topics table deletes the topic_search_data item (DeleteItem on topic_id) when a topic is removed or soft-deleted. No scan or batch sweep runs.
Delete all drafts of one user: Query on PK=user_id (user_id is the table's partition key), then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id (Query for keys, then delete each PK=user_id AND SK=draft_key)

access_patterns.description: Delete the search item of one user.
Fetch the anonymous account of a master user; the caller keeps the item only when its active attribute is true.
List all user field definitions ordered by position: Query on the single item collection, sorted by position in the application (14 items).
Fetch the cache record of one theme from the sparse JavascriptCacheByTheme index.
List the reviewables of one topic with a given type and status, filtered to one target creator, oldest first. Served by a Query on the topic GSI; target_created_by_id is a FilterExpression.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id AND SK=status AND type AND created_at ascending

access_patterns.description: Check that a badge exists and is enabled by id. GetItem on the badge; the application tests the enabled attribute on the returned item.
Read a full badge by id.
Look up one user action by action type, user, acting user, target topic and target post. The sort key action_key holds the four non-user parts, so it is a GetItem.
Insert a user action. The PutItem is rejected when an item with the same user and action_key exists, which replaces the source unique index.
Count the actions of one type created after a timestamp. Query with Select=COUNT on the action type GSI with a created_at range.
Read a full badge by id when it is enabled. GetItem; the application tests the enabled attribute on the returned item.

List the ids of reviewables with a status, score at or above a threshold and latest_score below a cutoff. Query on the status and score GSI with latest_score as a FilterExpression; the application sorts the ids descending.
List the ids of reviewables of one type and status created before a cutoff. Query on the status and created_at GSI with type as a FilterExpression.
Read a full badge by id with a row limit of 1.
Count the actions of one type. Query with Select=COUNT on the action type GSI.

Read the oldest reviewables of a status created before a cutoff, in id order with a limit. Query on the status and created_at GSI; the application orders the returned items by id and applies the limit.
Count the reviewables of a status with a score above a threshold. Query with Select=COUNT on the status and score GSI.

Consistency repair of target_topic_id, replaced by write-time enforcement: the write path that sets target_post_id sets target_topic_id in the same PutItem, and a post move updates the copies found through the UserActionsByTargetPost GSI with one conditional UpdateItem each.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id AND SK=action_key (items found by Query on GSI UserActionsByTargetPost, PK=target_post_id)

access_patterns.description: Duplicate clean-up, replaced by prevention: the natural key is the sort key and every insert is a conditional PutItem (pattern DDB-AP-160), so a duplicate is never stored. Duplicates already in the source are dropped by the migration load.
Delete every reviewable created by one user. Query on GSI ReviewablesByCreator (PK=created_by_id), then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned base keys, never a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: GSI ReviewablesByCreator PK=created_by_id, then delete PK=id

access_patterns.description: Delete every user action that refers to one user as the owner, target or actor. Query the base table (PK=user_id) and GSIs UserActionsByTargetUser and UserActionsByActingUser, then BatchWriteItem deletes of the returned keys, run where the user is deleted; never a Scan.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=user_id; GSI UserActionsByTargetUser PK=target_user_id; GSI UserActionsByActingUser PK=acting_user_id

access_patterns.description: Find the reviewable for a target by type, target type, target id and status. Query on the target GSI with status and target_type as sort key conditions.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=type AND target_id AND SK=status AND target_type

access_patterns.description: Insert one search log row; the application generates the id and writes the expires_at epoch attribute.
Read the password record of one user by user_id.
Insert one unsubscribe key; the key is the table partition key and an expires_at epoch attribute is written for TTL.
List the upcoming change names of one event type; the application orders the roughly 12 returned items by created_at.
List every job name already run. A Query on the constant onceoff_scope partition replaces the full table read; the table holds 91 items.
Fetch the events of one event type for up to 12 named upcoming changes with one BatchGetItem on the full keys; the application orders by created_at.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=event_type AND SK=upcoming_change_name (one key per name)

access_patterns.description: Read one webhook event type by id.
Update created_at and term of one search log by id; expires_at is recomputed from the new created_at in the same UpdateItem.
Read the modifier set of one theme by theme_id. The IS NOT NULL tests become attribute_exists checks on the returned item, because a column that is NULL has no attribute on the item.
Insert the password record of a user; one record per user is enforced by the user_id key.
Delete a password record. The caller holds the record it read, so it deletes by user_id and requires the id to match.
Insert a webhook event type with its explicit id.
Copy the hooks of one event type to another: a Query on PK=web_hook_event_type_id of the source type reads its items, and a BatchWriteItem puts them under the new web_hook_event_type_id.
access_patterns.key_condition: Query PK=web_hook_event_type_id (source type), then write items PK=web_hook_event_type_id (target type) AND SK=web_hook_id

access_patterns.description: Check whether a job name has already run, through the OnceoffByJobName index that returns keys only.
Record a job as run; the application generates the id.
Insert an upcoming change event. The key (event_type, upcoming_change_name) is the source's unique pair, so the conditional put enforces it.
Check only_theme_color_schemes of one theme: GetItem by theme_id, then compare the attribute in the application.
Retention delete served by Time to Live on expires_at (created_at plus the retention period); DynamoDB removes expired items in the background at no write cost.
access_patterns.key_condition: TTL attribute expires_at (system delete, no key condition)

access_patterns.description: Retention delete served by Time to Live on expires_at (created_at plus the retention period); DynamoDB removes expired items in the background at no write cost.
access_patterns.key_condition: TTL attribute expires_at (system delete, no key condition)

access_patterns.description: Read the modifier set of one theme by theme_id.
Read one site setting, every attribute, by its unique name.
Load all settings (name, data type, value) at once. Served as a Query on the AllSettings index, whose single partition value holds the whole 27-row table, instead of a Scan.
Read the value of one setting by name.
Delete a setting by name.
Rename a setting. The name is the table key, so the rename deletes the old item and puts the new one in one transaction; the put fails if the new name exists.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=name (old name: Delete with attribute_exists(name); new name: Put)
access_patterns.condition_expression: attribute_exists(name) on the old item AND attribute_not_exists(name) on the new item

access_patterns.description: Copy a setting under a new name: GetItem on the source name, then PutItem of its data type, value and timestamps under the new name with a new application-generated id.
Update a setting's value by its source id: a Query on SettingsById finds the name, then UpdateItem on that name.
Create a setting; the name key rejects a duplicate and the application generates the id.
Rename a setting only when the new name is free, as one transaction that deletes the old item and puts the new one.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=name (old name: Delete; new name: Put)
access_patterns.condition_expression: attribute_exists(name) on the old item AND attribute_not_exists(name) on the new item

access_patterns.description: Read one user's state for one topic by the full key.
Set last_emailed_post_number on one existing topic_users row. The item must exist, as in the source UPDATE, which never creates a row.
Read one user's state for several topics: a BatchGetItem of (topic_id, user_id) keys, one key per topic in the IN list.
access_patterns.key_condition: PK=topic_id AND SK=user_id, one key per topic in the IN list

access_patterns.description: Find the posts that a given reply post answers: Query the RepliesByReplyPost index on reply_post_id to get post_id values, then fetch those posts from the posts owner's table with a BatchGetItem by id and drop deleted ones. The posts fetch belongs to the posts owner.
List the users of a topic whose last_read_post_number is at least a value: Query the topic's partition with a FilterExpression on last_read_post_number.

Create a topic_users row. The (topic_id, user_id) key is the source's unique pair, so the Put is rejected when the item already exists. The application generates the id value the source took from a sequence.
Existence check on one topic_users row: GetItem by the full key; the application applies the notifications_reason_id null test and the notification_level range to the two returned attributes.
Existence check that a user has a given notification_level on a topic: GetItem by the full key with the level compared by the application.

Next unread post candidates of a topic: Query the posts TopicPosts index on topic_id with post_number greater than the user's last_read_post_number (read from topic_users by GetItem), limit 1, filtered on post_type and deleted_at. The reply_to_user_id and notification tests run in the application from a topic_users GetItem, a category_users GetItem, and a topic_tags Query on topic_id followed by tag_users GetItems.

Find the id of the post with a given post_number in a topic: Query the TopicPosts index with an equality on both key attributes, filtered on deleted_at and post_type, ordered by sort_order by the application.
Read every scope of one API key.
Find the account a user has with one provider.
Existence check for a live (not deleted) embed of a topic: Query on the topic_id GSI with the filter attribute_not_exists(deleted_at), Limit 1.
Upsert of a daily request counter: UpdateItem with ADD count creates the item when absent, replacing INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
Existence check for an enabled second factor of one method for a user: Query on the user with a filter on method and enabled, Limit 1.
Read every auth token of one user.
Read the non-revoked API keys of one user: Query on the user with the filter attribute_not_exists(revoked_at).
Read the new_email of a user's requests whose change_state differs from a given state: Query on the user with a filter on change_state.

migration_notes.application_logic_required: The source trigger raises an error on any insert or update that touches require_reply_approval. The application rejects writes to that attribute before it calls PutItem or UpdateItem.
The source trigger raises an error on any insert or update that touches require_topic_approval. The application rejects writes to that attribute before it calls PutItem or UpdateItem.

The trigger raises an error when topic_id is changed. DynamoDB has no triggers: the application writes topic_id once on PutItem and any UpdateItem on a timer leaves it out; an UpdateItem condition expression can also reject a topic_id change.

trade_offs.description: Each table is keyed by the column its in-scope queries look up by, so bookmarks, poll_votes, user_badges, quoted_posts, upload_references, topic_views, group_users and do_not_disturb_timings no longer use the source's generated id as their key.
trade_offs.impact: The id stays as an attribute. A lookup by that id alone needs a new index; the observed queries (`-1504869`, `-7736444`, `-2374558`, `-4538458`, `-5182200`, `-4017385`, `-8245385`, `8338762`) never do that, and the composite keys equal the source's unique indexes, so a duplicate row cannot be written.

trade_offs.description: The five set-based deletes by a key column (given_daily_likes, poll_votes and topic_views by user, quoted_posts by post, upload_references by target) are served as a Query on the partition key followed by BatchWriteItem deletes in batches of 25.
trade_offs.impact: A delete is no longer one statement: the application pages through the Query and retries unprocessed items. Each key value holds a small item set (the largest table has 90 rows), so a delete takes one Query page and one to a few batch calls. upload_references combines target_type and target_id into one partition key because the query supplies both; the delete never scans.

trade_offs.description: The tsvector column search_data of post_search_data is not migrated; the DynamoDB item keeps raw_data, locale, version and private_message.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB serves the key lookups by post id (query `-6123276`, 33 statements) as one BatchGetItem of at most 100 keys. Full-text matching on search_data stays on Aurora PostgreSQL, which absorbed the search workload and keeps the GIN index; the BatchGetItem path cannot rank or match text.

trade_offs.description: Tag names, tag slugs and tag group names are copied onto the category_tag_links items so the category tag lists need one Query and no join.
trade_offs.impact: The copies are written during migration. The observed workload has no tag or tag group rename; a rename would have to rewrite every link item that carries the name, and finding those items needs an index on tag_id or tag_group_id that is not built. The links are read at 0.0007 requests per second each.

trade_offs.description: The do-not-disturb check is a Query on user_id with the sort key (starts_at plus id) at or below now, then a filter on ends_at above now.
trade_offs.impact: The filter reads every item of the user with an earlier start, and those reads are billed whether or not they match. A user holds a handful of windows (the source table is 0.04 MB), so the cost is one read unit at most per check.

trade_offs.description: Existence checks on reviewable_scores (by score type) and user_badges (by badge and grant time) read KEYS_ONLY indexes, ScoresByType and BadgeGrantsByDate.
trade_offs.impact: Each index lags its base table until DynamoDB applies the write to it; the checks read nothing but key attributes and take the first match, so a score or grant written a moment before the check can be missed until the index applies it. The checks run at 0.0021 and 0.0002 requests per second; the score type has few distinct values but the load per value is far below the 3,000 RCU/s limit.

trade_offs.description: The source unique indexes on groups (name, incoming_email), tags (name) and category_settings (category_id) get no sentinel items; category_settings is keyed by category_id, so the key itself enforces it.
trade_offs.impact: No in-scope query inserts or changes groups or tags rows, so the load migrates once and no uniqueness check runs at write time. A write path added later for name or incoming_email needs a sentinel item inside a TransactWriteItems with attribute_not_exists.

trade_offs.description: Rows with a NULL user_id in poll_votes (nullable in the source) cannot be keyed by user_id; topic_views uses the viewer key USER#id, or IP#address when user_id is NULL.
trade_offs.impact: poll_votes rows without a user are not loaded and the migration reports their count; the delete by user never addressed them. topic_views keeps anonymous views under the address, so they stay reachable by key. Timestamps are stored as ISO 8601 strings.

trade_offs.description: Wide columns stay inline: groups averages 8156 bytes per row and api_keys 73400 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit; the row counts of bookmarks, category_settings, reviewable_scores, tags, topic_views and upload_references are derived from the table size.
trade_offs.impact: No item is near the limit, so no S3 offload or pointer attribute is added. Table item counts and the read figures for those tables rest on the size-derived counts and are small whichever way they are corrected.

trade_offs.description: No table or index carries load near a partition limit: the highest is post_search_data at about 0.13 RCU/s against 3,000 per key value, and the highest write is upload_references at 0.0229 WCU/s against 1,000.
trade_offs.impact: No shard suffix or time bucket is needed. The notifications table is keyed by its own id, so its write and read load spreads over all 158 items.

trade_offs.description: post_actions is keyed by user_id with the action id as sort key, and the user and post lookup runs on the ActionsByUserPost index.
trade_offs.impact: The key-scoped delete of all actions of a user (query `-1932152331896383119`) and the ordered read of a user's first actions (query `6946259433174667106`) are a Query on the base table. The user and post lookup (the 8 statements of the post_actions pattern, led by query `7574554412558242017`) reads an eventually consistent index that lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write. The table row count (11) is assumed because the source has no count; it is derived from the table's size over the item size.

trade_offs.description: ActionsByType uses the low-cardinality post_action_type_id as partition key for the existence check of query `-4753344182186834428`.
trade_offs.impact: The check issues a Query with Limit 1 at 0.0021 requests per second, far below the 3,000 RCU/s partition limit. The index keeps a type's actions in one partition, which is acceptable at the 11-row table size; the index must be sharded if the table grows to a rate near the limit. The index projects deleted_at so the filter on deleted_at absent runs on the index.

trade_offs.description: post_timings is keyed by topic_id with a composite sort key user_id#post_number, plus the PostTimingsByUser KEYS_ONLY index.
trade_offs.impact: The four full-key statements (queries `-2563491474259071174`, `9001219420538660836`, `9015066027187306476`, `9139176344923219931`) are single-item operations. The insert that ignores conflicts becomes a PutItem with attribute_not_exists, and the msecs increment becomes an UpdateItem with an atomic ADD conditional on the row existing. The delete by user (query `68093669830730243`, about 5 rows per user) reads keys from PostTimingsByUser, an index that lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write, then deletes in batches; a row written moments before the delete can be missed by one run.

trade_offs.description: user_emails keeps the surrogate-free key user_id plus EMAIL#id in an item collection rather than keying on the email address.
trade_offs.impact: No in-scope query looks emails up by address, and the source shows no unique index on email, so the address is not a key. Reads by user (queries `-154240961292348669`, `-3633820134551568594`, `-1103477891760818995`, `8884374594193225812`) are Queries on the user's partition with a primary filter; a user holds one or two items, so the filter discards at most one item. The 48-row table stays well under the 400 KB item limit (2,840 bytes average).

trade_offs.description: The unique index on (user_id, primary) of user_emails is enforced with a sentinel item UNIQ#PRIMARY#<primary> in the user's partition, written in the same TransactWriteItems as the email.
trade_offs.impact: The insert (query `8686349253882749431`) is a 2-item transaction with attribute_not_exists on both Puts, so a second primary email for a user cancels the transaction. The delete (query `-7887291093737212990`) removes the email and its sentinel in one transaction. Each transaction item costs two write units (prepare and commit), so the insert costs 4 write units for the roughly 1 KB record and sentinel, at 0.0012 requests per second. A GSI alone would not enforce the constraint.

trade_offs.description: UserEmailsById is a sparse-free INCLUDE index on email_id that serves the delete by id (query `-7887291093737212990`).
trade_offs.impact: The delete arrives with only the email id, so the application reads user_id and primary from the index (an eventually consistent read; a row created in the same second can be missing, and a strongly consistent GetItem on the base item is not possible without user_id) before the transactional delete. These lookups are 0.0011 requests per second against 0.3154 for the user-keyed reads, so the identifying key stays user_id.

trade_offs.description: The full read of badges.icon (query `-5609072216516021935`) is a Query on the BadgesAll index, whose partition key is the constant 'all'.
trade_offs.impact: A Scan is avoided. All 55 items share one partition key value at 0.0004 requests per second, so the load is far below the partition limit. The badges table is owned by another group; this group defines a placeholder with the id key and the attributes its two patterns read, and the merge folds it into the owner's table.

trade_offs.description: The topics placeholder serves two GetItem reads (queries `6746886374591153495`, `6004114026531250967`); the deleted_at IS NULL filter becomes an application check on the item.
trade_offs.impact: GetItem has no filter expression, so the application drops an item whose deleted_at attribute is present. The placeholder defines only topic_id, title, slug and deleted_at; the source reads SELECT *, so the owner group's table must carry the full item (2,641 bytes schema size, 2,374 bytes measured). The two patterns total 0.5269 requests per second, and the topics placeholder does not write the table.

trade_offs.description: Query `4582415969089977699`, a UNION of existence probes over post_actions and reviewable_scores, is not given an access pattern (query type OTHER).
trade_offs.impact: It runs 0.0002 requests per second and reads reviewable_scores, which another group owns; the probes map to the ActionsByType index for the post_actions half. The application issues each probe as its own Query.

trade_offs.description: posts is keyed by topic_id and post_number instead of the surrogate id, with the PostsById index on id.
trade_offs.impact: Queries `5773944441398922381` and the query pattern holding `-5186433891132204782` (about 1,500 reads per hour) address a post by topic and number, while the id lookups (queries `5294935299087107482`, `-4105318780350388611`, `-4931816337163920361` and `-9104347101806609042`, about 1,750 reads per hour) use the index. (topic_id, post_number) is unique in the source and not nullable. A post moved to another topic is a delete and a put of the item. Other groups that read posts by id stay served by PostsById.

trade_offs.description: PostsById projects ALL attributes because the id reads return the full post (53 attributes) and no in-scope query writes posts.
trade_offs.impact: The index stores a second copy of each 2,886-byte item (728 items) and every future post write is applied to both. No read needs a base-table fetch. Index reads are eventually consistent: a post just written can be absent from PostsById until DynamoDB applies the write to it, and a caller that must see it reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem on topic_id and post_number.

trade_offs.description: The deleted_at IS NULL and post_type IN (...) conditions run as FilterExpressions (GetItem and BatchGetItem results are checked by the application), and the sort_order ordering is applied by the application.
trade_offs.impact: A filter does not reduce read capacity: deleted posts are read and billed before they are dropped. Each id lookup returns at most one item, so ordering by sort_order needs no sort key.

trade_offs.description: The text columns raw, cooked and raw_email stay inline in the post item.
trade_offs.impact: The posts table averages 2,809 bytes per row (2,886 bytes by schema) against the 400 KB item limit, so no value is moved to S3. A post whose raw, cooked and raw_email together exceed 400 KB would be rejected on write.

trade_offs.description: users is a placeholder owned by group 0, keyed by id, with three indexes this group's queries need: UsersByUsername (ALL), UsersByUsernameLower (KEYS_ONLY) and UsersByUploadedAvatar (KEYS_ONLY, keyed on the nullable uploaded_avatar_id).
trade_offs.impact: The merge keeps the owner's key schema and folds these indexes into its users table. username and username_lower are unique in the source, but no in-scope write inserts or changes them, so no sentinel item is written; the indexes are read paths only. UsersByUploadedAvatar holds only users that have an avatar; the share of users without one is not measured, so its item count is the upper bound of 53.

trade_offs.description: The two UPDATE statements on users (`2150880814507944816` and `8321624443266976557`) are served at write time, not as set-based sweeps.
trade_offs.impact: The avatar orphan clean-up runs when an upload is deleted: a Query on UsersByUploadedAvatar finds the referencing users and a conditional UpdateItem clears each reference. The title repair runs when a badge, a user's badge grant or the profile's granted_title_badge_id changes, and uses the keys that groups 3, 5 and 9 define for badges, user_profiles and user_badges. The users writes in this group target the owner's table; the owner group still designs all other writes to it. Every PutItem on users must carry the union of both groups' attributes.

trade_offs.description: Topics, uploads and user profiles keep the source surrogate id as the table key. topics.external_id and uploads.sha1 are unique but nullable, so they are not keys.
trade_offs.impact: A null external_id or sha1 cannot be a partition key value, and a PutItem on a duplicate key silently overwrites an item. The id stays the key and the id is reachable for other groups' lookups; external_id is not read by any query in scope.

trade_offs.description: sidebar_section_links is keyed by user_id and a link_key of '<linkable_type>#<linkable_id>', the natural unique key (user_id, linkable_type, linkable_id), and optimized_images by upload_id and a variant of '<width>x<height>#<extension>', the natural unique key (upload_id, width, height, extension). Both are unique on the source's evidence (unique indexes on NOT NULL columns) and immutable in the queries.
trade_offs.impact: The surrogate id of each table becomes a plain attribute. A conditional PutItem with attribute_not_exists on the key replaces the source's unique-index conflict handling, so no sentinel items are needed for these two tables.

trade_offs.description: uploads.sha1 is unique and the upload insert writes it, so the insert is one TransactWriteItems of 2 items: the upload and a sentinel item in upload_sha1_sentinels, with attribute_not_exists(sha1) on the sentinel Put.
trade_offs.impact: A taken sha1 cancels the whole insert. Each of the 2 items costs two writes (prepare and commit) at 0.0001 requests per second, and a canceled transaction still consumes them. The UploadsBySha1 index serves eventually consistent lookups only and never enforces uniqueness.

trade_offs.description: The database generated the id of uploads, optimized_images and sidebar_section_links; the application now generates these ids before the write.
trade_offs.impact: The insert statements no longer return a generated id. The application allocates ids from a unique source and carries the id in every PutItem.

trade_offs.description: Three global secondary indexes serve lookups the base keys cannot: UploadsByUrl (url, upload_id range), UploadsBySha1 (sha1) and SidebarLinksBySection (linkable_type and sidebar_section_id, position order). All project ALL because the reads return the whole item.
trade_offs.impact: Index reads lag the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to the index; a caller that needs the latest write reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem. Each upload write also writes two index entries. SidebarLinksBySection holds only links that carry a sidebar_section_id; the sidebar link insert (query `-4963619`) leaves it unset.

trade_offs.description: The upload url query adds conditions on created_at and retain_hours and an id cursor. The index Query keys on url and the id range; the retention and cutoff conditions run as a FilterExpression.
trade_offs.impact: A filter does not reduce read capacity, but one url has a single upload (rows returned 0 on average), so the filter adds no measurable cost.

trade_offs.description: The topic reads by id use BatchGetItem for the IN list (7.5 ids on average, at most 100 per call) and GetItem for single ids. The deleted_at IS NULL and archetype conditions are evaluated by the application on the returned item, because a deleted_at attribute is absent when null.
trade_offs.impact: Items with deleted_at set are fetched and dropped by the application; they cost read capacity. The archetype existence check becomes a GetItem followed by an application comparison.

trade_offs.description: The optimized_images update by id (query `-929154033288984175`) addresses the item by upload_id and variant, taken from the loaded record; no index on the surrogate id exists.
trade_offs.impact: A caller that holds only the optimized image id must first read the upload's images with a Query on upload_id. The source's update is by id alone; this design assumes the record is loaded first. 0.0002 updates per second are affected.

trade_offs.description: The consistency repair sweep (query `2539559289466738950`) that clears granted_title_badge_id where the user's title is empty is modeled at write time: the write path that changes a user's title issues a conditional UpdateItem on that user's profile. users is owned by another design group, which designs its writes; this group defines no write to users.
trade_offs.impact: Until the users writes call the profile update, profiles can keep a badge reference after the title is cleared, with no bound. The sweep is not run as a Scan plus batch write; one UpdateItem per affected profile carries attribute_exists(granted_title_badge_id).

trade_offs.description: user_profiles (avg_row_size_bytes 2572) and uploads (2294) keep their capped text columns (location, website, origin) inline.
trade_offs.impact: Both sizes are far below the 400 KB item limit, and bio_raw and bio_cooked are read with the profile in the same GetItem. Each profile read costs 0.5 read units per 4 KB.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for optimized_images (33) and uploads (9) are derived from the tables' data size over the item size.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts, sentinel counts and index item counts for these tables rest on that derivation, not on a collected count.

trade_offs.description: The users table keeps the source id as its key (`user_id`) and serves the lookup by lower-cased username through the UsersByUsernameLower index.
trade_offs.impact: Lookups by username (query `7551067` at about 3.3 requests per second) read the index, which is eventually consistent; lookups by id (queries `5575144`, `2274020`, about 1.2 requests per second together) read the base table. Username is unique and not null in the source, but a user can be renamed and a DynamoDB key cannot be updated in place, so the username stays an index key. Other design groups read users by id, so the id stays the table key.

trade_offs.description: Unique usernames and secure identifiers are enforced with sentinel items in the user_unique_values table, written in the same TransactWriteItems as the user, each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(unique_value).
trade_offs.impact: A user insert is one transaction of 1 + 2 items (the user, a username_lower sentinel, and a secure_identifier sentinel only when the value is present); each item costs two write units per KB, and a canceled transaction still consumes them. The username_lower sentinel also covers username, because two names that differ only in case share one lower-cased value. Deleting a user deletes its sentinels in the same transaction. The visible update (`-439324` pattern) changes neither unique column; an update that renames a user must delete the old sentinel and put the new one in its transaction. A GSI alone would not stop two concurrent sign-ups from taking the same name.

trade_offs.description: muted_users becomes its own table keyed by user_id and muted_user_id; the join to users in the muted-users list is dropped because the list returns only the muted user's id, which the key already holds.
trade_offs.impact: The list is a single Query on the muting user's partition (about 0.11 requests per second). The source join also dropped muted rows whose user no longer exists; the table has no foreign key, so deleting a user needs the application to delete that user's muted rows (a Query on the user's partition plus batch deletes). A member that also returns usernames adds a BatchGetItem on the users table for the muted ids. muted_users has no collected row count, so item_count is 0 from the stated assumption, which derives it from the 0.02 MB table size over the 292-byte item.

trade_offs.description: theme_fields is keyed by theme_id with the sort key field_key = target_id#type_id#name, the source's unique key, so the insert is a PutItem guarded by attribute_not_exists(theme_id).
trade_offs.impact: The full unique key is a GetItem and a target_id lookup is a begins_with Query. Reads by name or type_id alone, and name lists, are Queries on the theme's partition with a FilterExpression: filtered items still consume read capacity, which is acceptable because a theme holds about 69 items (155 rows in total) and the pattern rates are under 0.03 requests per second. Ordering by name and id in query `7649042` is done by the application on about 12 items.

trade_offs.description: The ThemeFieldsById index (KEYS_ONLY) maps a theme field's id to its table key for the value_baked update.
trade_offs.impact: The update (query `8669704`, about 0.0045 requests per second) is an UpdateItem on the base key; a caller holding only the field id first queries the index, which is eventually consistent and lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write. The index adds one write per field insert and key change, a few writes per hour in total.

trade_offs.description: The id columns of users and theme_fields were generated by the database (sequences, returned by INSERT ... RETURNING); the application now generates them.
trade_offs.impact: The application assigns the next user id (the table key) and field id before each insert, from a counter item or a snowflake-style generator, because DynamoDB has no sequence. Existing ids migrate unchanged.

trade_offs.description: theme_fields keeps its text columns (value, value_baked) inline.
trade_offs.impact: The table's average row is 3,383 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so the columns stay inline and no S3 offload is needed; a theme field above 400 KB would fail the write.

trade_offs.description: Reads by id (`GetItem`, `BatchGetItem`) are eventually consistent and users are updated in place with a condition that the item exists.
trade_offs.impact: A read right after an UpdateItem on the same user can return the old item until the write replicates, within one second; the updater itself gets the new item from ReturnValues=ALL_NEW without a read. Callers that need the latest value set ConsistentRead on the base-table read.

trade_offs.description: The three DELETE statements by model_id (queries `-1435330` `524039068` `499176814` as embeddings cleanups) are served by keying each embeddings table on model_id with a composite sort key of strategy and entity id.
trade_offs.impact: A model removal is a Query on one partition key followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of 25 items per call, not a set-based DELETE. The unique source index (model_id, strategy_id, entity id) becomes the table key, so no sentinel items are needed. A bulk removal must be paced below the 1,000 WCU/s limit of one key value; each table holds 19 items today at 541-558 bytes per item.

trade_offs.description: The embeddings column (halfvec) is stored as a binary attribute and the 19-row tables carry no vector search query in this group.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB stores the vector bytes but cannot run similarity search on them. The measured average item is 558 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so the vector stays inline. Any nearest-neighbour read stays on the engine that serves vector search.

trade_offs.description: group_requests and reviewable_claimed_topics deletes by user_id (queries `45187686` and `60515295`) run as a Query on a KEYS_ONLY GSI keyed on user_id plus BatchWriteItem deletes.
trade_offs.impact: The GSI lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so a delete issued right after a new insert can miss the new item; the application re-runs the delete or reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem. The GSI adds one write per base write, 0.0006 WCU/s at design rate. group_requests keeps its id as key because group_id and user_id are nullable in the source unique index; items with a null user_id are absent from the GSI.

trade_offs.description: reviewable_claimed_topics is keyed on topic_id instead of the surrogate id because topic_id is unique and NOT NULL in the source (one claim per topic).
trade_offs.impact: A claim is unique by key without a sentinel item. A topic cannot be re-keyed in place; changing it is a delete and a put. The table holds 0 rows today, so the user_id GSI is empty until claims are created.

trade_offs.description: external_upload_stubs gets a GSI on status (partition) and created_at (sort) for the retention delete (query `11537686`), which is a status plus time-range filter with no key value.
trade_offs.impact: The delete becomes a Query with status equality and created_at at or before the cutoff, then batched deletes by id, never a Scan. status has few distinct values, so one status value holds most index items; at 15 items and 0.0003 requests/s the load is far below the 1,000 WCU/s and 3,000 RCU/s per-key limits, so no shard suffix is added. A table that grows to millions of stubs needs the status value sharded (for example `status#0..9`) with one Query per shard.

trade_offs.description: The category_posting_review_groups lookup (query `-7096413`) is keyed on category_id with a sort key of post_type#group_id, and the IN list of 8 categories becomes 8 Queries.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the 8 Queries in parallel and merges the results; each uses begins_with on the post type. The source unique index (category_id, group_id, post_type) is NOT NULL on all columns, so it becomes the table key and the surrogate id is kept only as an attribute.

trade_offs.description: The llm_models listing (query `-7865273`) has no filter, so it is served by a GSI whose partition key is the constant attribute catalog and whose sort key is id.
trade_offs.impact: All 10 items live under one index key value, which is acceptable at 0.0002 requests/s and 10 items; growth to thousands of models keeps the Query under the 1 MB page limit. The index projects display_name, so the read needs no base-table fetch. api_key is stored as a plain attribute copied from the source column, and the migration needs to encrypt or move it to a secrets service.

trade_offs.description: theme_svg_sprites is keyed on theme_id and user_uploads on (user_id, upload_id) because the source unique indexes are NOT NULL and the queries `28794562` and `-29379276` look them up by exactly those columns.
trade_offs.impact: Both lookups are GetItem calls. The sprite bytea stays inline: the table's measured average is 345 bytes against the 400 KB item limit. The row counts of all tables in this group are derived from table size, not collected.

trade_offs.description: No in-scope write inserts or changes a unique attribute, so no sentinel items are created.
trade_offs.impact: The group has only DELETE statements; inserts of these tables run in other parts of the application. Any later insert path that relies on the source unique indexes already gets uniqueness from the table keys chosen here, except group_requests (group_id, user_id) and external_upload_stubs.key, which need a sentinel item written in a TransactWriteItems with attribute_not_exists once an insert is designed.

trade_offs.description: problem_check_trackers is keyed on the natural pair identifier and target instead of the generated id.
trade_offs.impact: The pair is unique in the source (a unique index on non-null columns), is read by every pattern and is never changed in place, so reads by pair are GetItem and Query on the partition key, and the insert carries `attribute_not_exists(identifier)`. The update `4578670901435518703` addresses the tracker by identifier and target, which the application already holds; the id stays as an attribute.

trade_offs.description: The tracker row averages 4033 bytes (details JSON), under the 400 KB item limit, and stays inline as a map attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Each read or write of a tracker costs one 4 KB read unit or 4 write units; with 13 rows the table holds about 52 KB.

trade_offs.description: The unique indexes on post_custom_fields.post_id and topic_timers.timerable_id and topic_id are not enforced with sentinel items; both tables are keyed with the generated id as sort key.
trade_offs.impact: The collected index entries show no predicate, but their names (notice, stalled wiki trigger, missing uploads ignored, public type and deleted_at) mean they are partial indexes over specific names or states, and the predicate text is not in the evidence. A sentinel on post_id alone would block a post from holding several fields. The insert `-3970536631062481956` is a conditional put on `attribute_not_exists(id)`, which reproduces ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING only for the same id; per-name uniqueness rests on the application until the predicates are confirmed.

trade_offs.description: topic_timers is keyed on the string timerable_key (type and timerable_id) with id as sort key.
trade_offs.impact: Queries `9075088` and `5617716` name type and timerable_id by equality, so one Query reads the item collection; deleted_at, public_type and status_type are filter expressions over at most a few items per key, and the filter does not reduce read units but the collection is small.

trade_offs.description: Due timers are read from the sparse index DueTimersByType (partition key active_type, sort key execute_at), where active_type is written only while deleted_at is null.
trade_offs.impact: Deleted timers are not indexed, so the index holds only active timers. The source orders by id; the index returns execute_at order and the application sorts the few results by id. The index lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write; the due-timer poll tolerates that lag. The partition key is the low-cardinality type, which is safe at 0.09 reads per second over 13 rows. The two statements that write topic_timers are outside this group, so the group does not design the write that sets or removes active_type; the owner of those writes maintains it.

trade_offs.description: category_custom_fields gets the index CategoryFieldsByName (partition key name, sort key value, keys only) for the lookup of categories by field name and value.
trade_offs.impact: The redesign requirement for query `-3475673` is met by a Query on this index instead of a Scan. The cardinality of name is unknown; at 0.0009 reads per second the key value carries no hot-partition risk. A KEYS_ONLY index returns category_id, which the query reads, so it needs no base-table fetch. The sort key holds value, so a value over 1024 bytes cannot be indexed.

trade_offs.description: The IN-list reads on post_custom_fields and category_custom_fields (up to 7 names and up to 7 categories by 10 names) become a Query per partition key with a name filter expression.
trade_offs.impact: The source returns rows by id order across categories; DynamoDB runs up to 7 Queries for query `-4224723` and the application merges them. Filters do not reduce consumed read units, but each partition holds under 1 KB of data on average, so the cost is one read unit per Query.

trade_offs.description: The scheduler_stats retention delete `5139002051034385017` is served by Time to Live on an expires_at epoch-seconds attribute (started_at plus the retention period) set at insert.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background at no write cost, within a few days of expiry rather than at the cut-off second; the 82657-row table is never scanned. The retention period is not in the collected evidence and is set by the application. A read that must not see an expired run filters on expires_at. A DynamoDB Streams consumer can archive the deleted runs.

trade_offs.description: scheduler_stats keeps the application-generated numeric id as partition key; the source sequence is replaced by an id the application generates.
trade_offs.impact: Writes are 1.93 WCU per second spread over unique id values, so no key value is hot. The completion update uses `attribute_exists(id)` and reads nothing back; the source RETURNING id is replaced by the generated id the application already holds.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for category_custom_fields (38) and topic_timers (13) are derived from the tables' data size over the item size.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and storage figures for these two tables rest on that derivation; both tables are under 0.1 MB, so the figures do not change the design.

trade_offs.description: The source tables carry no tenant column, so partition keys do not lead with a tenant attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Item-level isolation by `dynamodb:LeadingKeys` is not available for these tables; isolation stays in application code, as in the source.

trade_offs.description: topic_custom_fields is keyed by topic_id with the sort key name#id, not by topic_id and name alone.
trade_offs.impact: The source index on topic_id and name is not unique, so a topic can hold several rows with one name; the id suffix keeps each row as its own item. Reads by name (query `6932753489`) become a Query with begins_with on the name prefix, one per requested name, and the application merges the results. The table holds 19 items of about 545 bytes, so one topic partition is far below the 400 KB item and 10 GB partition limits.

trade_offs.description: Four tables switch from the generated id to a natural key: translation_overrides (locale, translation_key), plugin_store_rows (plugin_name, key), topic_voting_topic_vote_count (topic_id) and watched_words (action, then id as sort key).
trade_offs.impact: Each natural key is unique in the source through a unique index on non-null columns (topic_id is nullable, so a vote count row without a topic is not migrated), and each is the column its reads filter on, so reads are a GetItem or Query with no index. The id stays as a plain attribute. watched_words keeps the id as sort key because the unique index is on (action, word) and its list read orders by id. Key attributes cannot be updated in place: a changed locale, key or topic is a delete plus a put. Other groups are not recorded as reading these tables by id.

trade_offs.description: badge_types and color_schemes keep the generated id as partition key.
trade_offs.impact: Their reads (queries `41950144` and `-68487856`) look up by id. badge_types has a unique name index, but no in-scope read uses the name, so no index is added. Query `-3852732` also tests remote_copy; GetItem cannot filter, so the application compares the returned remote_copy flag and discards a mismatch, which costs the same read as the unfiltered lookup.

trade_offs.description: schema_migrations uses a constant partition key (ledger) with version as sort key.
trade_offs.impact: The only read lists every version in order (query `31790646`), so all 2284 items of about 82 bytes (roughly 190 KB) sit in one partition and one Query pages through them in sort-key order. The read rate is 0.0007 per second and the write rate 0.0264 per second, against partition limits of 3000 read and 1000 write units per second. The insert (query `2680313`) carries attribute_not_exists(version), so a version recorded twice is rejected by the table key itself and needs no sentinel item.

trade_offs.description: The skipped_email_logs retention delete (query `-5145007`) becomes Time to Live on an expires_at epoch attribute written with each log item.
trade_offs.impact: The source DELETE removes rows with created_at older than a cut-off, which on DynamoDB would be a Scan plus batch deletes. DynamoDB instead deletes expired items in the background at no write cost, typically within days of expiry, not at the second. The item gets expires_at equal to created_at plus the retention period, which the application sets from its cut-off setting. Reads that must not see an expired item filter on expires_at; no in-scope read targets this table. A DynamoDB Streams consumer can archive removed items. The table keeps an application-generated numeric id as key because the log is write-only in scope.

trade_offs.description: user_notification_schedules gets a sparse index EnabledSchedules keyed on enabled_marker, an attribute written only while enabled is true.
trade_offs.impact: Query `-6710918` reads every enabled schedule; a filter on a base-table Query would read every item, so only the enabled items are indexed instead. DynamoDB key attributes cannot be booleans, hence the string marker. The share of items excluded is not measured because the source has no row count (derived from table size, assumed 0 rows), so the exclusion percentage is unknown; enabled defaults to false in the source, which makes most items excluded. The index projects all attributes because the read returns the whole item. Every write that changes enabled adds or removes the index item. The index is eventually consistent and lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; the per-user read (query `6915433`) reads the base item. The table row counts in this group (for example 40 skipped email logs, 19 topic custom fields) are derived from table size.

trade_offs.description: No sentinel items are written for the unique indexes on badge_types.name, watched_words (action, word) and the topic_custom_fields partial unique indexes.
trade_offs.impact: No in-scope query inserts or changes those values, so they are loaded once by the migration and need no transaction. A later write path that inserts into those tables must add a sentinel item per unique value in one TransactWriteItems call with attribute_not_exists, which costs two write units per item.

trade_offs.description: The text columns (topic_custom_fields.value, plugin_store_rows.value, skipped_email_logs.custom_reason, translation_overrides.original_translation) stay inline in their items.
trade_offs.impact: The tables' average row sizes are between 280 and 545 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, so no value moves to S3 and no pointer attribute is needed.

trade_offs.description: The user_fields full scan (query `-2453444`) becomes a Query on one item collection with the constant partition key field_scope, and the position-ordered read (query `3003621`) sorts its 14 items in the application.
trade_offs.impact: All 14 field definitions live under one partition key value. At 0.0561 reads per second and about 10 KB per read the load is far below the 3,000 read units per second limit, and the application sorts by position after the Query.

trade_offs.description: drafts is keyed on the natural pair user_id and draft_key instead of the generated id, because the source has a unique index on (user_id, draft_key) over non-null columns and every read and the delete by user (query `33950506`) address it.
trade_offs.impact: A PutItem on the pair replaces the same draft, as the source's unique index did. The delete of all drafts of a user is a Query on the partition key followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of at most 25 keys per call. The source id is kept as an attribute and no pattern in this group reads drafts by it.

trade_offs.description: javascript_caches is an item collection with sentinel items for the unique theme_id and the unique (theme_field_id, name) pair, which the insert (query `79675277`) writes with the record in one TransactWriteItems of at most 3 items, each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(cache_key). The record is keyed by the application-generated id.
trade_offs.impact: A taken theme_id or name pair cancels the insert. Each transaction item costs two writes, so an insert of a 2,330-byte record with two 1 KB-or-smaller sentinels costs about 10 write units at 0.0011 inserts per second. The sentinels are only written when the value is present, as the source allows several NULL values. The item_count includes up to two sentinels per record.

trade_offs.description: The id of javascript_caches was generated by the database and is now generated by the application, because the item key JSCACHE#{id} must exist before the transaction is sent.
trade_offs.impact: The application allocates a unique id for each cache record, for example a UUID or a counter item, before the insert.

trade_offs.description: The theme lookup (query `24832854`) reads the sparse JavascriptCacheByTheme index keyed on theme_id with ALL projection; only records with a theme_id are indexed.
trade_offs.impact: The index lags the base item until DynamoDB applies each write to it. Uniqueness comes from the THEME sentinel, never from the index. The index holds the 99 records that carry a theme_id, so records without one are not indexed.

trade_offs.description: tag_users has the TagUsersByLevel index on (user_id, notification_level) with KEYS_ONLY projection for the tag id lookup (query `-2955284`).
trade_offs.impact: The index returns only tag_id, which is a table key attribute, so no base-table fetch is added. Each notification_level change deletes and reinserts the index entry, which doubles the index write for that update.

trade_offs.description: The tag_users and topic_tags subquery (query `-5481939`) is split: the application reads the tag ids of the topic from the owner of topic_tags, then calls BatchGetItem on tag_users for those keys, filters levels 3 and 4 and sorts them descending.
trade_offs.impact: Two requests replace one SQL statement. A topic with more than 100 tags needs several BatchGetItem calls. The group does not write topic_tags and defines no index on it.

trade_offs.description: allowed_pm_users copies the username of the allowed user from users into each item, replacing the join in query `-4829209`.
trade_offs.impact: When a user renames, the owner of users must update the copies, which are found by the reverse unique pair (allowed_pm_user_id, user_id) that this group does not index. Until the copy is updated the old username is returned. The group does not write users.

trade_offs.description: polls is keyed on post_id and the poll id as sort key, so both reads by post (queries `-4457441` and `-3763155`) are a Query and the ORDER BY id comes from the sort key.
trade_offs.impact: Polls with a NULL post_id cannot be keyed by post and need a different home if any exist; the source has no row count for them. Reads by poll id alone are not served by this table, and the unique pair (post_id, name) is not enforced because no in-scope write inserts polls.

trade_offs.description: anonymous_users is keyed on master_user_id, which has a unique index over a non-null column, and the active = true condition of query `11714267` is checked on the returned item.
trade_offs.impact: GetItem cannot filter, so the application discards an item whose active attribute is false. The unique user_id is not indexed because no in-scope query reads by it.

trade_offs.description: The tsvector columns search_data of topic_search_data and user_search_data are not stored; only raw_data, locale and version are written by the upserts (queries `34182582` and `76836928`).
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB cannot hold or query a tsvector. Full-text search over these rows runs on Aurora PostgreSQL, which remains in the target architecture. The raw_data stays inline: the measured average row is 1,555 bytes for topic_search_data and 2,176 bytes for user_search_data against the 400 KB item limit.

trade_offs.description: The orphan clean-up of topic_search_data (query `-1857846`) is modeled as a DynamoDB Streams consumer on the topics table that deletes the search item by topic_id, in place of the source's join-and-delete sweep.
trade_offs.impact: The owner of topics must enable a stream with REMOVE and soft-delete events (deleted_at set) for the consumer; this group does not write topics. A deletion is applied after the stream record is delivered, which is within seconds, and until then the search item is still readable by key.

trade_offs.description: The shared_drafts IN-list reads (nine statements, pattern PAT-8) become BatchGetItem on topic_id; the source lists up to 36 ids per statement.
trade_offs.impact: BatchGetItem takes up to 100 keys and 16 MB per call, so one call serves each list. Keys that have no draft are absent from the response.

trade_offs.description: The source has no row count for allowed_pm_users, anonymous_users, shared_drafts, tag_users, drafts and polls, so their item_count values come from the table sizes in design_metrics.
trade_offs.impact: Capacity figures for these tables rest on derived row counts (0 for tables under 0.03 MB, 20 for drafts and 11 for polls); they are recomputed from real counts at migration.

trade_offs.description: All reads of user_stats (queries `-4271916` and `-8871138`) and all single-key lookups are eventually consistent GetItem calls.
trade_offs.impact: A read made right after a write to the same key can return the previous item for the duration of replication, normally under one second; a caller that must see its own write reads with ConsistentRead set to true.

trade_offs.description: user_actions is keyed by user_id with the natural key (action_type, acting_user_id, target_topic_id, target_post_id) as the sort key `action_key`, and the surrogate id stays a plain attribute.
trade_offs.impact: The lookup by the five-column key (query `2647612`) becomes a GetItem and every insert is a conditional PutItem, so the duplicate rows that the source clean-up (query `-2784383`) removes cannot be stored. The source unique index allows several rows with NULL parts; a NULL part is written as 0, so two such rows now collide on one item. No query in this group looks a user action up by id.

trade_offs.description: The unique constraint on user_actions is enforced by the primary key itself with attribute_not_exists(action_key) on the PutItem, so no sentinel item is written.
trade_offs.impact: An insert costs one write; a rejected duplicate returns ConditionalCheckFailedException and the application treats it as already recorded.

trade_offs.description: The duplicate clean-up (query `-2784383`), the consistency repair of target_topic_id (query `-8208700`) and the delete by any of three user references (query `3015126`) are modeled by their target-native approach, not as a Scan plus batch write.
trade_offs.impact: Duplicates are prevented at insert. The topic id is set in the same write that sets the post id, and moving a post updates the copies found through GSI UserActionsByTargetPost.
