Deleting a user queries the base table and the target-user and acting-user GSIs and deletes the returned keys with BatchWriteItem, run where the user is deleted. The posts rows that the repair reads belong to another design group, so the application supplies topic_id from the post when it writes the action.

trade_offs.description: Counts of user_actions (queries `-8883206` and `-2719095`) and reviewables (query `1175638`) are Query calls with Select=COUNT on a GSI keyed by the counted column.
trade_offs.impact: Each count reads and bills every matching item: user_actions holds 1025 items at 140 bytes in GSI UserActionsByType, and reviewables holds 9 items (derived from the table size). At 0.0032 to 0.0095 calls per second this costs under 0.01 read units per second; a counter item maintained with an atomic ADD in the write transaction replaces the Query if the table grows by orders of magnitude.

trade_offs.description: Five GSIs on reviewables and four on user_actions serve the status, topic, target, creator, action type and user-reference lookups, with KEYS_ONLY for the delete and count paths, INCLUDE of latest_score for the score filter, and ALL for the full-row reads.
trade_offs.impact: Each insert writes to every GSI. At 0.0156 inserts per second on user_actions this adds four index writes per insert and about 0.06 write units per second. No read returns attributes missing from its index, so no base-table fetch is needed.

trade_offs.description: ReviewablesByStatus, ReviewablesByStatusScore and UserActionsByType have a low-cardinality partition key (status, action_type).
trade_offs.impact: All items of one status or action type sit in one key value. Peak load is under 0.03 read units per second against a 3000 limit, so no shard suffix is used; a table growing to hundreds of reads per second on one status needs a fixed shard suffix on the key and a Query of every shard.

trade_offs.description: ORDER BY id on the reviewables reads (queries `2643383` and `5026464`) is done by the application, because the GSI sort key is score or created_at.
trade_offs.impact: The application sorts the returned items by id and applies the LIMIT after reading the matching range; with 9 reviewables this reads one page.

trade_offs.description: GSI reads are eventually consistent and lag the base item until DynamoDB applies the write to the index.
trade_offs.impact: A reviewable or user action written just before a GSI Query can be absent from that result; a read that needs the latest write uses a GetItem on the base key with ConsistentRead.

trade_offs.description: Badges stay a single table keyed by id (55 items, 882 bytes each); badge name is unique and non-null in the source but no query in this group reads by it.
trade_offs.impact: All eight badge query ids are GetItem calls on id; the application checks the enabled flag on the returned item. The average row of 1907 bytes is far below the 400 KB item limit, so description, long_description and query stay inline.

trade_offs.description: The reviewables payload JSON column is stored as a map attribute, and the reviewables row count of 9 is derived from the table size of 0.08 MB over the item size.
trade_offs.impact: Capacity figures for reviewables rest on that derived count. The payload is parsed on load and written back as a map.

trade_offs.description: Queries `-5857369` (delete of topic_users by user_id) and `931558391` (update of topic_users notification_level by user_id) write topic_users, which another design group owns, so this group defines no access pattern for them.
trade_offs.impact: The owning group designs the user_id lookup that both writes need (a partition key or GSI on user_id), and these two statements are served there. This group adds no placeholder table or index for topic_users.

trade_offs.description: The retention deletes on search_logs (query `3022359024859565856`) and unsubscribe_keys (query `9113575919552827162`) become Time to Live on an expires_at epoch attribute, written as created_at plus the retention period on every insert.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background with no write cost, within days of expiry rather than at the second. A read that must not see an expired item filters on expires_at. The retention period is the value the application's cleanup job uses today; the migration sets it when it backfills expires_at.

trade_offs.description: onceoff_logs keeps a constant partition key onceoff_scope with the generated id as sort key, so the list-all read (query `-7989811519127883198`) is a Query and not a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: All 91 items share one partition. At 0.0091 requests per second reading about 34 items of 250 bytes, the load is far below the 3,000 read units per second partition limit, and the table stays small, so the single partition is acceptable.

trade_offs.description: onceoff_logs gets the OnceoffByJobName index (KEYS_ONLY) for the existence check by job_name (query `1472164085369536536`); job_name is nullable and not unique in the source, so it is not the table key.
trade_offs.impact: The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a job that must see its own just-written log reads the item through the base table by id. The index holds only items that have a job_name and costs one extra write per insert (0.0004 per second).

trade_offs.description: Ids the database generated (search_logs.id, onceoff_logs.id) are generated by the application, and the inserts carry attribute_not_exists(id).
trade_offs.impact: The application supplies a unique numeric id on each insert (such as a time-ordered id generator). Sequences no longer exist, and ids are not gap-free or consecutive.

trade_offs.description: upcoming_change_events is keyed by the natural unique pair (event_type, upcoming_change_name), the source's unique index on non-null columns, not by the surrogate id; the id stays as an attribute.
trade_offs.impact: A conditional PutItem enforces the pair's uniqueness without a sentinel item. The ORDER BY created_at of queries `-6058845784046842780` and `3093312870194031514` is applied by the application on about 12 returned items, and the IN list of 12 names becomes one BatchGetItem on full keys. The key cannot be updated in place, so renaming a change is a delete and a put.

trade_offs.description: user_passwords and theme_modifier_sets are keyed by user_id and theme_id, the unique non-null columns their reads use, instead of the surrogate id; the id stays as an attribute. The password delete (query `-5476648005661698537`) addresses the item by user_id with the condition id = :id.
trade_offs.impact: Lookups by user_id (query `-8450912255165174963`) and theme_id (queries in the PAT-16 pattern) are single GetItem calls. A second password row for a user cannot exist, as in the source. There is no index on the surrogate id; reads by id alone are not served by this design.

trade_offs.description: The IS NOT NULL and equality filters on theme_modifier_sets (queries `-1911262412598852204` and `5076669123351474512`) are evaluated by the application on the GetItem result, since a NULL column has no attribute on the item.
trade_offs.impact: Each read returns the single 572-byte item for the theme and the application checks attribute_exists or the boolean value. The read cost is one item read per call, the same as an unfiltered lookup.

trade_offs.description: The INSERT ... SELECT copy on web_hook_event_types_hooks (query `2584108843483812003`) is a Query on the partition web_hook_event_type_id followed by a BatchWriteItem under the target type id; the table is keyed by (web_hook_event_type_id, web_hook_id), the source's unique pair.
trade_offs.impact: The copy is not atomic: BatchWriteItem is at most 25 items per call and the application retries unprocessed items. The row count of the table is assumed (the source has no count), so the batch count per copy is not measured.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for onceoff_logs, theme_modifier_sets, upcoming_change_events, web_hook_event_types and web_hook_event_types_hooks are derived from each table's size, because the source has no count for them. search_logs.user_agent (declared up to 2000 bytes, counted at 1 KB in the item size) stays inline: the table's average row is 195 bytes against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and the capacity figures that rest on them are approximate; the loads are far below the partition limits at any plausible count. The user_agent column needs no S3 offload.

trade_offs.description: Password reads (query `-8450912255165174963`) are strongly consistent GetItem calls on the base table.
trade_offs.impact: A read right after a password change or reset sees the latest hash. Each strongly consistent read of the 502-byte item costs 1 read unit instead of 0.5, about 0.057 read units per second at design load.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed on the setting name instead of the source id: the name is unique and NOT NULL (unique index index_site_settings_on_name), 27 distinct values over 27 rows, and 6 of 9 patterns look rows up by name.
trade_offs.impact: Uniqueness of the name is enforced by the table key itself, with no sentinel item. A rename changes the key, so it is a delete of the old item plus a put of the new one in one TransactWriteItems (2 items, 4 write units per rename at about 5 renames per hour). The source id stays reachable through the SettingsById index for the update by id.

trade_offs.description: The id-based update (query `-1896810`) first queries SettingsById for the name, then runs UpdateItem on that name.
trade_offs.impact: SettingsById is a global secondary index, so it lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; an update by an id created in the same instant can find no row and the application retries after the write is visible. Update by id runs at 0.0004 requests per second, so the extra read costs 0.0002 read units per second.

trade_offs.description: The unfiltered read of all settings (query `-5236333`, no WHERE) becomes a Query on AllSettings, whose partition key is the constant attribute scope = SITE, holding all 27 rows, instead of a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: All items share one partition key value on that index. At 0.0014 requests per second returning about 31 items of about 300 bytes, the load is far below the 3,000 read units per second partition limit, so no sharding is applied. The index is eventually consistent and lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write.

trade_offs.description: Generated ids move to the application: the source's serial id has no DynamoDB counterpart, so the insert and the copy (INSERT ... SELECT) write an application-generated id.
trade_offs.impact: The copy reads the source item by name with GetItem and puts a new item under the new name with attribute_not_exists(name); two concurrent copies to the same name leave one item. The value column is TEXT with an average table row of 1942 bytes, far under the 400 KB item limit, so it stays inline.

trade_offs.description: topic_users is keyed by topic_id (partition) and user_id (sort) instead of the generated id; the source's unique (topic_id, user_id) pair becomes the primary key.
trade_offs.impact: Every topic_users read and write in this group names both topic_id and user_id, or only topic_id, so the pair is the natural key and no GSI is needed. A PutItem carries attribute_not_exists(topic_id), so a duplicate pair is rejected rather than overwritten, and no sentinel item is needed because the table key itself is the unique constraint. The pair never changes after creation. The id column stays as a plain attribute that the application now generates in place of the sequence behind query `6765621213240346328`.

trade_offs.description: The id values that the source database generated for topic_users and topic_tags are generated by the application.
trade_offs.impact: Query `6765621213240346328` returned the new id with RETURNING; the application now assigns the id before the PutItem and uses it as an ordinary attribute.

trade_offs.description: The filter on last_read_post_number in query `-2081487299388086276` is a FilterExpression on the Query of one topic's partition.
trade_offs.impact: The Query reads every user item of the topic and bills all of them, because a filter does not reduce read capacity. The table holds 726 topic_users rows with 881 bytes per item, so one topic's collection stays far below the 1 MB page; a topic with thousands of readers needs a GSI on topic_id and last_read_post_number.

trade_offs.description: The IN list of topic ids in the PAT-6 reads becomes a BatchGetItem of up to 100 (topic_id, user_id) keys, and the notification_level and notifications_reason_id predicates of queries `-3292419205471075412` and `-6617783115228636850` are evaluated by the application on the item returned by GetItem.
trade_offs.impact: Each call returns up to one item per requested key; a key with no item is simply absent, and unprocessed keys must be retried by the caller. The predicates add no read cost because GetItem bills the item once.

trade_offs.description: Query `5884248130138369695` joins post_replies to posts; DynamoDB serves it as a Query on the RepliesByReplyPost index followed by a BatchGetItem of the posts by id, with the deleted_at IS NULL test applied by the application.
trade_offs.impact: The read takes two requests instead of one join. The index is KEYS_ONLY because it returns only post_id; the posts fetch is billed to the posts owner's table. The index reflects a reply row once DynamoDB applies the write to it and is eventually consistent; a caller that must see a reply it just wrote reads post_replies by its base key, post_id and reply_post_id. post_replies has no primary key in the source and both key columns are nullable, so the migration loads only rows where post_id and reply_post_id are both present.

trade_offs.description: Query `-5272548625492493566` is served by several requests: a Query on the posts TopicPosts index, a GetItem on topic_users, a GetItem on category_users, and a Query on topic_tags followed by GetItems on tag_users.
trade_offs.impact: The source evaluates the unread-post conditions in one SQL statement; the application now runs the sub-lookups and applies the OR of reply_to_user_id, topic notification_level, category notification_level and tag notification_level itself. category_users (group 7) and tag_users (group 8) are designed by their owners and are read by their own keys; this group adds no pattern that writes them and defines no index depending on their writes. The query runs 0.004 times per second, so the extra requests add under 0.01 read units per second. The posts placeholder carries only the attributes this group reads; the owner's table holds the rest, and every PutItem on a post carries the union of both groups' attributes.

trade_offs.description: topic_tags is keyed by topic_id and tag_id and has no index on tag_id; the posts placeholder is keyed by id with a TopicPosts index on topic_id and post_number.
trade_offs.impact: No query in this group looks topic_tags up by tag, so the reverse (tag_id, topic_id) index of the source is not created; the sub-lookup in query `-5272548625492493566` is a Query on the topic_id partition. Any pattern from another group that reads posts by topic and number uses TopicPosts. The posts key schema stays with its owner; the merge keeps the owner's keys and maps this index onto them.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for post_replies and topic_tags are not collected, so their item counts are 0 in this draft.
trade_offs.impact: Their capacity figures rest on the table sizes in design_metrics (0.02 MB each for post_replies and topic_tags) and on the sub-1 KB item sizes of 240 and 286 bytes; at that size a read of one item bills 0.5 read units.

trade_offs.description: ai_agents has a unique name that the insert `7964039920894090174` sets, so the insert writes the agent and a name sentinel item in one TransactWriteItems call, each Put guarded by attribute_not_exists(ai_agent_key).
trade_offs.impact: A duplicate agent name cancels the whole insert, as the relational unique index did. Each insert is 2 items in the transaction (limit 100) and costs two writes per item, prepare and commit. A rename deletes the old sentinel and puts the new one in the same transaction. The agent and its sentinel share the ai_agents table as an item collection.

trade_offs.description: ai_agents stays keyed by the surrogate id (AGENT#id) because the read `-9107418073878310695` looks agents up by id; name is unique and not null but no in-scope read uses it.
trade_offs.impact: Lookups by id are a GetItem. A lookup by name is a GetItem on the sentinel followed by a GetItem on the agent, using the id the sentinel carries.

trade_offs.description: ai_agents rows average 3755 bytes (system_prompt is declared up to 10,000,000 characters), far below the 400 KB item limit, so system_prompt, description and tools stay inline. The table has 36 rows, derived from the table's size.
trade_offs.impact: No S3 offload is needed at the measured size. A system_prompt that grows toward 400 KB moves to S3 with a pointer attribute. A read of one agent costs 1 read unit at 4 KB rounding.

trade_offs.description: application_requests is keyed by its unique natural key (date, req_type) and web_crawler_requests by (date, user_agent); the generated id stays as a plain attribute. Both tables are small counters read and written by that key only. The upsert `6668674146221133871` becomes an UpdateItem with ADD count.
trade_offs.impact: The upsert is one atomic UpdateItem with no read-then-write race. Each table has one partition per date; at 0.2 writes per second there is no hot key. date and req_type are stable, so no key is ever rewritten.

trade_offs.description: sitemaps is keyed by its unique, non-null name because the read `-8729198876356079750` looks it up by name; the id stays as an attribute. The table has 3 items, and its measured average row size of 17476 bytes comes from page overhead, so the schema size of 178 bytes is used.
trade_offs.impact: The lookup is a GetItem on name. A rename of a sitemap is a delete and a put of the item.

trade_offs.description: Inserts into schema_migration_details, post_stats and color_scheme_colors (queries `-4917791749421847216`, `5423936073563966392`, `-8362095136812523352`) used database-generated ids; the application now generates the id and each PutItem carries attribute_not_exists(id).
trade_offs.impact: The application needs a unique numeric id generator. A duplicate id fails the write instead of overwriting an item.

trade_offs.description: The GSIs AssociatedAccountsByProviderUser (provider_name, user_id), TopicEmbedsByTopic (topic_id), DirectoryColumnsByName (name, type) and ScreenedIpByActionType (action_type, last_activity_at) serve queries `-7832492340302674463`, `2931539718557711172`, `1217360975432785261` and `-5195588254230218940`. The first, third and fourth project all attributes because their reads return the whole item; TopicEmbedsByTopic projects only deleted_at for its filter.
trade_offs.impact: GSI reads are eventually consistent: an index lags its table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, and the read that must see a write immediately uses the base table. The tables are written rarely in scope, so the extra index writes are negligible. Unique source indexes on these columns are not enforced on DynamoDB: no in-scope write sets them, so no sentinel is written, and a later write path has to add one.

trade_offs.description: The query `-5195588254230218940` tests last_match_at < cutoff OR (last_match_at IS NULL AND created_at < cutoff); the design stores last_activity_at (last_match_at, or created_at when never matched) as the GSI sort key and reads it with one range condition. action_type has few distinct values and the table 50 items.
trade_offs.impact: This equals the source filter when both branches use the same cutoff, as the source does. last_activity_at changes whenever last_match_at changes, which moves the item inside the index. At 0.0002 reads per second the low-cardinality partition key carries no measurable load.

trade_offs.description: Filters on non-key columns are applied as FilterExpressions after a Query on the user: user_second_factors (method, enabled; query `763652916241229345`), user_api_keys (attribute_not_exists(revoked_at); query `7661205089442229807`), email_change_requests (change_state not equal; query `-2135502268557629957`) and directory_columns (icon absent; query `1217360975432785261`).
trade_offs.impact: A filter does not reduce the read units, which are charged for every item the Query reads. Each user holds a handful of such items (15 second factors, 16 API keys and 17 change requests in the whole table), so the filtered items add no measurable cost.

trade_offs.description: The query `5571699630796892942` reads every embeddable host with no filter; the design stores all 22 items under the constant partition key embeddable_scope = ALL and reads them with one Query instead of a Scan. The query returned 0 rows on average in the collector, so 22 items (the table's row count) are used for sizing.
trade_offs.impact: The whole set is one partition: 22 items of about 486 bytes cost about 2 read units per call at 0.02 calls per second, far below the 3000 read units per second limit. The set stays small; a growth past a few thousand items needs a sharded key or a cache.

trade_offs.description: Row counts for ai_agents, api_key_scopes, directory_columns, email_change_requests, embeddable_hosts, screened_ip_addresses, topic_embeds, user_api_keys, user_associated_accounts, user_auth_tokens and user_second_factors are derived from each table's size, because the collector has no count for them. The read rates for these tables are unmeasured peaks (peak factor 1).
trade_offs.impact: Item counts and capacity figures for these tables are derived from table size over the schema item size; each is a few dozen items, so capacity is not sensitive to the figure.

trade_offs.description: The user-scoped tables category_users, dismissed_topic_users, draft_sequences, user_options, user_security_keys and user_visits share one item collection, `user_data`, keyed by user_id with a typed sort key.
trade_offs.impact: Every read in this group names a user, and the three deletes by user_id (queries `7717599755018108916`, `-5142529018510995284`, `4287094098748345668`) become a Query on a sort-key prefix plus BatchWriteItem in groups of 25, never a Scan. Each source table keeps its own sort-key prefix, so rows from different tables never collide.

trade_offs.description: The source unique indexes on (category_id, user_id), (user_id, visited_at), (user_id, draft_key), (user_id, topic_id) and user_options.user_id are enforced by the table primary key (user_id plus sort key), and user_options inserts carry `attribute_not_exists(user_id)`.
trade_offs.impact: A duplicate insert is rejected by the table itself, so these writes need no sentinel items and no transaction. The unique credential_id of user_security_keys is not enforced: no in-scope query inserts or changes it, and the one-time load writes it as an ordinary attribute.

trade_offs.description: discourse_solved_solved_topics is keyed on topic_id instead of the surrogate id, because every read looks a topic up by it and the source holds a unique index on topic_id over a NOT NULL column.
trade_offs.impact: Lookups are GetItem and BatchGetItem on the key. The source id stays an attribute with no index, so another group that reads this table by id would need its own GSI. The answer_post_id unique index has no in-scope writer and gets no key.

trade_offs.description: The category notification lookup of query `4253263512682689512` joins topics through a subquery; the application reads the topic's category_id from the topics owner's item and then issues a GetItem on the category row.
trade_offs.impact: The lookup costs one extra GetItem on the topics table owned by another group, and the notification-level filter and ordering run in the application. This group adds no write or index on topics.

trade_offs.description: SELECT DISTINCT user_id over dismissed_topic_users (query `8521344751852874806`) is served by the sparse GSI DismissedUsers, keyed on a constant marker that only dismissed items carry.
trade_offs.impact: The index holds only dismissed items (every other item in `user_data` is excluded), and the application removes duplicate user ids from the Query result. All index items sit under one partition key value; at the observed 0.0002 reads per second this is far below the 3,000 RCU/s limit, and a higher read rate would need a shard suffix on the marker. The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it.

trade_offs.description: The UPDATE of query `6213645647369225488` that appends text to details cannot run as one statement; it becomes a Query on the ActorActions GSI (acting_user_id, projecting details) with an action filter, then one conditional UpdateItem per record.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB has no string concatenation in an update expression, so the application writes details as the value it read plus the suffix, guarded by `details = :previous_details`; a concurrent change makes the update fail and the application retries it. Each update also rewrites the ActorActions entry because details is projected there. The statement is rare (0.0006 per second).

trade_offs.description: user_histories gets two GSIs, ActorActions (acting_user_id, action) and TargetUserActions (target_user_id, action, created_at), each projecting only the attributes its read uses.
trade_offs.impact: The existence check of query `-4634586055388130285` filters on previous_value and new_value, which TargetUserActions projects, so it never fetches the base item. Each insert of a history record writes to both indexes, three writes in total, at 0.0009 inserts per second. Queries on these indexes are eventually consistent.

trade_offs.description: The visit count of query `-5378124675010793632` is a Query with Select=COUNT on the user's visit range (SK greater than the date) with a filter on posts_read.
trade_offs.impact: The Query reads and bills every visit item in the range, at most one item per day per user, 295 bytes each, so a year of visits is about 100 KB. A counter item is not used because the count has a date and a posts_read threshold as parameters and runs 0.0003 times per second.

trade_offs.description: A user_options item is 3,300 bytes by the schema (the measured average row is 7,490 bytes), against the 400 KB item limit, so it stays inline in one item.
trade_offs.impact: A read of the options item bills 1 read unit of 4 KB at most (0.5 eventually consistent); a full write bills 4 write units. The query `2385444039654002092` pattern returns all 67 columns, so no projection narrows it.

trade_offs.description: The source generates ids for user_histories rows (RETURNING id) and the other tables; the application generates the id of each new user_histories item before PutItem.
trade_offs.impact: The id is unique per item and guarded by `attribute_not_exists(id)`. The application replaces the database sequence with a time-ordered unique id such as a UUID or a ULID, and no ordering by id is used by an in-scope query.

trade_offs.description: Telemetry reports 0 returned rows for most key lookups, and row counts are assumed for category_users, dismissed_topic_users, discourse_solved_solved_topics and user_visits; the design prices each key lookup at one item and treats existence checks as returning none.
trade_offs.impact: Read units in `hot_partition_analysis` are an estimate at those assumptions. All figures stay far below the partition limits (under 1 percent), so a different row count does not change the keys.

trade_offs.description: The security-key existence check of query `5146492642468846180` is a Query on the factor-type prefix with a filter on enabled and a limit of one item.
trade_offs.impact: The filter runs after the read, so the check reads all keys of that factor type for the user (13 rows exist in total). Reads that must see a just-enabled key use a strongly consistent Query on the base table.

trade_offs.description: Categories, their category_groups rows and their category_featured_topics rows share one item collection keyed by category_id, with sort keys META, GROUP#group_id#id and FEATURED#topic_id.
trade_offs.impact: The visibility check (query `8344127436710142645`) reads the category and its group permissions in one Query, and deleting a category's featured topics (query `974806976840491591`) is a Query plus BatchWriteItem on one partition. The surrogate ids of the featured-topic rows are not part of the key: (category_id, topic_id) is unique in the source and becomes the sort key, so the id column is not migrated.

trade_offs.description: The categories table has avg_row_size_bytes of 20972 against a schema item size of 3088; description and topic_template stay inline as text attributes.
trade_offs.impact: Every category item stays far under the 400 KB item limit, and each GetItem reads one 4 KB unit or a few more; no S3 offload is needed.

trade_offs.description: The visibility check joins category_groups to group_users for the caller's groups. The category and its group rows come from one Query on categories; the caller's group ids come from the owner group's design of group_users, and the application intersects the two sets.
trade_offs.impact: The single SQL statement becomes two reads and an application-side check; this design adds no placeholder for group_users because it only reads it and the owning group designs its key.

trade_offs.description: Reads that return a whole small table in order (all featured topics by rank, all flags by position, all theme ids) use an index whose partition key is the constant ALL, written only on the items each read returns.
trade_offs.impact: These indexes hold 36 featured topics, 40 flags and 35 themes at 0.0004 to 0.0061 requests per second, far below the 3,000 read and 1,000 write units per key value, so the single partition value is not a hot key; a table that grows by orders of magnitude needs a sharded suffix.

trade_offs.description: Invites and invited_users form one item collection keyed by invite_id; InvitedUsersByUser (sparse on redeemed_at, keys only) finds a user's redeemed invites and InvitesByEmail (sparse on email, all attributes) finds invites by email, with deleted_at filtered after the read.
trade_offs.impact: Query `-3983690881457160113` is an index Query plus a BatchGetItem of invite items, and the application orders by invite id; the source measured 0 rows returned, so the fetch adds 0 read units at design rate. Index entries lag the base table until DynamoDB applies each write; the redemption path that must see a new redemption reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: user_custom_fields is keyed by user_id with sort key name#id, not by (user_id, name): the source's unique indexes on (name, user_id) are partial indexes for specific names, and the plain (user_id, name) index is not unique.
trade_offs.impact: A user can keep several values under one name, as the source allows. The name IN (...) read (query `-6794419130351561971`) becomes one Query per name with begins_with, and results are ordered by id in the application.

trade_offs.description: The cross-user update of a custom field value (query `2866689475356927595`) is a Query on CustomFieldsByNameValue (partition key name and value) followed by an UpdateItem per item. The value column is text and a key attribute holds at most 2048 bytes for a partition key.
trade_offs.impact: A value longer than 2048 bytes is not indexed and cannot be found by this update; changing value rewrites the index entry (a delete and a put). At 0.0001 requests per second the extra write cost is below 0.001 write units per second.

trade_offs.description: Query `7771545769178583636` deletes sidebar_section_links rows by user_id, a table the group 5 design owns. This draft defines a placeholder with the owner's key (PK user_id, SK link_key) so the delete is a Query on the base table plus BatchWriteItem instead of a Scan.
trade_offs.impact: The placeholder uses the owner's key schema, so the merge keeps it unchanged. The delete only removes items by key and sets no flag on a context table.

trade_offs.description: Generated integer ids (categories.id, flags.id, themes.id, invites.id) stay as the item keys, and the application generates ids for new rows.
trade_offs.impact: Sequences have no DynamoDB equivalent; new category, flag, theme and invite ids come from the application or a counter item. Key lookups by the source id keep working for other groups' placeholders.

trade_offs.description: The admin_notices delete by subject and identifier is served by a NoticesBySubjectIdentifier GSI keyed on both columns, projecting details.
trade_offs.impact: The delete runs as a Query on the GSI, a filter on details, then one DeleteItem per match, instead of one SQL statement. Each delete also writes the GSI, so the write cost doubles at 0.017 writes per second. The GSI lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a delete that must not miss a just-written notice re-reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem.

trade_offs.description: The reviewable_histories delete by created_by_id is served by a keys-only HistoryByCreator GSI followed by BatchWriteItem deletes of up to 25 items per call.
trade_offs.impact: The delete becomes a Query plus batched deletes, not one statement, and each delete also removes the GSI entry. The GSI lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write to it, so entries written just before the delete may need a second pass.

trade_offs.description: Child tables are keyed by their parent or lookup column plus the unique partner column, and the source surrogate id stays as a plain attribute: ai_agent_mcp_servers (ai_agent_id, ai_mcp_server_id), category_required_tag_groups (category_id, tag_group_id), group_category_notification_defaults (group_id, category_id), group_tag_notification_defaults (group_id, tag_id), group_mentions (post_id, group_id), theme_site_settings (theme_id, name).
trade_offs.impact: The source unique indexes on these pairs become the DynamoDB primary key, so PutItem enforces uniqueness without sentinel items. Lookups by the surrogate id alone need a new GSI; no query in this group uses one. group_mentions.group_id is nullable in the source, so an item without a group_id cannot be written and the migration skips such rows.

trade_offs.description: permalinks, developers and push_subscriptions key on their natural lookup column (url, user_id) instead of the surrogate id; theme_settings, push_subscriptions and post_hotlinked_media use the lookup column as partition key and the id as sort key.
trade_offs.impact: permalinks.url and developers.user_id are unique and not null in the source, so a PutItem on the key cannot overwrite another row; a permalink url change is a delete and a put. The existence checks become a GetItem or a Query with Limit 1 on the key. The surrogate id remains an attribute only.

trade_offs.description: The category_required_tag_groups read ordered by the order column is a Query on the category_id partition; the application sorts the items by the order attribute.
trade_offs.impact: A category holds only a few required tag groups, so sorting in the application costs nothing measurable and avoids making the mutable order column part of the key, which would turn every reorder into a delete and a put.

trade_offs.description: The whole-table reads of custom_emojis (ordered by name), site_setting_groups and topic_voting_category_settings use a constant partition attribute (emoji_scope, setting_scope, voting_scope) with the name or category_id as sort key, so they are Queries and never Scans.
trade_offs.impact: All items of each table live in one partition. Each table holds 29, 37 and 0 rows at 0.0002 to 0.0014 requests per second, far below the 3,000 read units per second partition limit. The sort key also enforces uniqueness of name and category_id. topic_voting_category_settings.category_id is nullable in the source, so rows without a category_id are skipped by the migration.

trade_offs.description: The theme_site_settings read with two theme ids becomes two parallel Query calls, one per theme_id, and the sidebar_urls read of 12 ids becomes one BatchGetItem.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the requests and merges the results; the IN list has no single-request form in DynamoDB. BatchGetItem accepts up to 100 keys, so the 12-id read fits in one call.

trade_offs.description: backup_metadata ids come from a PostgreSQL sequence in the source and are generated by the application in DynamoDB; the insert carries attribute_not_exists(id).
trade_offs.impact: The application generates the id before the PutItem, and the conditional write rejects an id collision. The RETURNING id clause is replaced by the id the application already holds.

trade_offs.description: Item sizes stay inline: the largest is permalinks at 2476 bytes and then sidebar_urls at 1371 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit. Row counts for every table are derived from the table size, because the source has no counts for them.
trade_offs.impact: No column moves to S3. Capacity figures rest on the derived row counts, and all Query calls with zero collected rows are sized at one returned item.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed by the natural unique key (target, digest) instead of the surrogate id; the id stays as an attribute and is generated by the application.
trade_offs.impact: The source's unique index on target and digest is unique on non-null columns, so a conditional PutItem enforces uniqueness and no sentinel item is needed. The id sequence no longer exists; the application assigns increasing ids, and no other group reads this table by id.

trade_offs.description: The newest-ids read and the delete of older ids for one target use the GSI StylesheetsByTargetAndId (target, id) with a KEYS_ONLY projection; the delete queries the index and then removes items by table key with BatchWriteItem.
trade_offs.impact: The index adds one small item write per insert (about 122 bytes against a 75,215-byte table item) and lags the table until DynamoDB applies each write; the id read returns only keys, and the delete removes items by the table keys the index returns.

trade_offs.description: The retention delete (query `-6072012279523579697`) is served by Time to Live on an expires_at epoch attribute set to created_at plus the retention period, not by a Scan and batch delete.
trade_offs.impact: TTL deletes at no write cost within days after expiry, not at the second; a read that must not see an expired stylesheet filters on expires_at. The retention period is not in the query telemetry and is set by the application when it writes the item.

trade_offs.description: The content column stays inline: the table's average row is 75,215 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and 52 rows total 3.73 MB.
trade_offs.impact: Each insert costs about 74 write units and each existence-check GetItem reads up to 19 four-KB units, at under 0.004 requests per second, so cost is negligible. A stylesheet that grows past 400 KB would need to move to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: Ids that the source database generated from a sequence are generated by the application.
trade_offs.impact: The insert no longer returns an id from the database; the application creates it before the PutItem.

trade_offs.description: The table is keyed on token_hash instead of the source's surrogate id, because token_hash is unique and not null in the source, stable, evenly distributed (97 distinct values in 97 rows) and the key of the token confirmation lookup.
trade_offs.impact: A conditional PutItem with attribute_not_exists(token_hash) enforces the unique index without sentinel items, in one write. The id stays reachable through the TokenById index, which holds keys only.

trade_offs.description: Deleting a token by id (query `85658365`) and confirming a token by id (query `-8086318`) look up token_hash in TokenById with a Query, then write the base item. The two id-only writes run at 0.0012 requests per second together, against 0.0006 for the token_hash read, so the id index is the minority path by key rate.
trade_offs.impact: Each id-only write costs one extra index read of 0.5 read units and is a second request. TokenById lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write; a token created a moment ago may be missing from it until that write lands, and a caller that holds the token_hash skips the index.

trade_offs.description: The source's retention delete (query `-805676`) of unconfirmed, expired tokens past a cut-off becomes Time to Live on expires_at_epoch, written as created_at in epoch seconds plus the retention period only while confirmed is false and expired is true.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB deletes the items within days of the expiry time, at no write cost, and no Scan or batch write runs. A read that must not see an expired token filters on expires_at_epoch. The retention period is the cut-off the application passes as the delete's parameter and must be set in the migration's ETL; an update that confirms a token removes the attribute.

trade_offs.description: The query `3689045540` that expires a user's other tokens runs as a Query on the TokensByUser index (partition key user_id) with a filter on scope and id, followed by one UpdateItem per returned item.
trade_offs.impact: The write is no longer one SQL statement; it is a Query plus one UpdateItem per token, and it is not atomic across tokens. TokensByUser is eventually consistent, so a token written just before the call can be missed until the index applies the write.

trade_offs.description: Three GSIs are added: TokensByEmail (email), TokensByUser (user_id, email) and TokenById (id). The first two project all attributes because their reads return the full item; TokenById projects keys only because it only finds the token_hash for a write. Updates of expired and confirmed do not change any index key.
trade_offs.impact: Each insert writes the item four times (the table and three indexes) and each non-key update writes the table and the two ALL indexes; at 0.0018 writes per second the cost is negligible. No index key is mutable, so no delete and insert pair occurs on update.

trade_offs.description: The id column was generated by a database sequence; the application now generates it and writes it as an attribute.
trade_offs.impact: The id must stay unique across tokens; TokenById does not enforce uniqueness, so the generator carries it.

trade_offs.description: Items stay inline: the table's avg_row_size_bytes is 1405 and the schema item size is 417 bytes, against the 400 KB item limit, and the table has no TEXT or BLOB columns.
trade_offs.impact: No S3 offload is needed for this table.
